entities.summary:
The Hellenistic period was a transformative era in classical antiquity, spanning from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC to the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC. This global phenomenon was characterized by the widespread influence of Greek leadership, culture, and language across the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, as a result of Alexander's conquests. The period witnessed the rise of new city-states, the establishment of the Ptolemaic and Seleucid dynasties, and the development of new philosophical and scientific schools. Notably, the Hellenistic period was marked by the establishment of the Library of Alexandria, one of the largest and most significant repositories of knowledge in the ancient world.

    The Hellenistic period played a significant role in shaping the course of Western civilization, laying the groundwork for the Roman Empire's ascendancy in the Mediterranean. The period's cultural achievements, including the spread of Greek language and art, had a lasting impact on the development of Western philosophy, science, and politics. Furthermore, the Hellenistic period's legacy can be seen in the many cultural and architectural achievements of the period, including the construction of the Great Library of Alexandria, the establishment of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt, and the development of new scientific and philosophical schools.

    The Hellenistic period also had a profound impact on the social and political landscape of the ancient world. The period witnessed the rise of new city-states, the establishment of the Ptolemaic and Seleucid dynasties, and the development of new forms of governance and administration. Notably, the Hellenistic period saw the emergence of new social classes, including the growing middle class, and the development of new forms of artistic expression, including the rise of Greek tragedy and comedy.
